IPL 2027 predictions: Model A vs Model B

Model A (explainable): each team's strength is its form win % over the last 3 seasons (weights 3, 2, 1); team A beats team B with chance A / (A + B). Model B (machine learning): logistic regression and gradient boosting, averaged, using only pre-season information: Elo rating, last-10 form, head-to-head, ground record, home ground, squad strength and the Impact Player era. Both play the 2027 season 10,000 times in the real 10-team format (two groups of 5, 14 league games each, then Qualifier 1, Eliminator, Qualifier 2 and the Final).

Model A favourite (22.5% title chance)Royal Challengers Bengaluru
Model B favourite (20.7% title chance)Royal Challengers Bengaluru
Orange Cap (most runs): A / BB Sai Sudharsan (both)
Purple Cap (most wickets): A / BB Kumar (both)

Model A: why each team got its strength

A team's strength is its win % over the last 3 seasons, with the latest season counting 3 times. Royal Challengers Bengaluru: (3 × 68.8 + 2 × 73.3 + 1 × 46.7) ÷ 6 = 66.6. A season a team did not play is skipped, so only the seasons it played count.

What the models cannot know

  • Auctions, trades and releases. Both models read data/squads_2027.csv, which starts as each franchise's 2026 players. Edit it after the auction and run the pipeline again.
  • Injuries and availability during the season.
  • Breakout players. V Suryavanshi scored 252 runs in 2025 and 776 in 2026 to win the Orange Cap; before that season, Model A had him #44 and Model B had him #61 in the Orange Cap list. Past numbers cannot see a jump like that coming.
  • T20 is close to a coin flip before a ball is bowled. In the 2021-2026 backtest Model A picked 51.2% of winners and Model B 50.7%, against 50% for a coin flip, and neither beat the coin flip's log loss (0.6931). Treat the title chances as rough guides, not certainties.

Pitch and player fit

How each ground plays, and how it suits a particular batter, bowler or fielder. Note: the data has no pitch reports (grass, cracks, soil) or ball-tracking, so "how the pitch plays" is measured from what happened there: runs, wickets, fours and sixes, and dot balls, compared with the whole league in the same seasons (100 = average), so the 2026 scoring boom does not make newer grounds look flatter. This mixes the pitch with boundary size, outfield and weather.

How this ground suits a player

The player at this ground against the same player at other grounds in the same seasons (all seasons he played here).

Trends

Scoring inflation

Points table (rebuilt from the results)

2 points for a win, 1 for a no-result; NRR from the ball data (a team bowled out counts 20 overs). Rain-shortened matches use the overs actually bowled.

Chase win-probability calculator

A logistic regression trained on every ball of every normal chase in the data (see the chase chart below).

Season impact scores

Runs weighted by how hard scoring was in that phase, plus wickets worth the average runs per wicket in that phase (see docs/Code_Explanation.md).

One player's impact score by season

Match centre

Every match ball by ball: scorecard with dismissals and bowling card, an over-by-over strip, and the raw ball rows. Open the match centre →

Key insights

  • Chasing wins more: teams batting second won 54.5% of matches.
  • The toss hardly matters: the toss winner won 51.4% of matches.
  • Death overs (16-20) are the fastest scoring phase: 10.1 runs per over.
  • Gujarat Titans have the best all-time win rate: 61.0%.
  • Best single season: V Kohli scored 973 runs in 2016.
  • Since the Impact Player rule, the average first-innings score rose from 167.0 (2020-22) to 189.7 (2023-26), and 200+ totals from 0.21 to 0.67 per match.
